young.html: About five hundred years ago, the most famous teacher in Europe was a Dutchman named Erasmus. One summer, while staying with his friend Thomas More in London, he wrote a funny little book. In it, a character named Folly (which means foolishness) stands up in front of a crowd and gives a speech praising... herself!

Folly says everyone needs her. Friends get along because they overlook each other's silly habits. Parents think their children are the most wonderful in the world. People laugh, play and fall in love, and all of that, she says, is a little bit foolish. Then she teases all sorts of grown-ups who think they are very wise.

young.name: gb-folly
young.cap: Folly in the middle, and the kinds of people she teases. Tap a group.

young.html: The trick of the book is that we never quite know when to believe Folly. Sometimes she is just being silly. Sometimes she says something true that a serious person would not dare to say.

A speech in praise of something silly. Pick something small and silly (a sock with a hole, a squeaky door, a puddle) and write five sentences praising it as if it were the most important thing in the world. Read it aloud in a grand voice. Did any of your jokes turn out to be a little bit true?

full.html: Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536) was born in Rotterdam, trained as a priest, and became the leading humanist of northern Europe: a scholar who went back to the Greek and Latin classics, and to the earliest texts of the Bible, to renew learning and Christian life. He wrote in Latin, the shared language of educated Europe, and his books sold everywhere the new printing presses reached.

In 1509, riding back from Italy to England, he thought up a speech for Folly. He wrote it at Thomas More's house and dedicated it to More; the Latin title, Moriae Encomium, means "The Praise of Folly" and also puns on More's name. It was printed in 1511 and became one of the best sellers of the century.

full.text: At what rate soever the world talks of me (for I am not ignorant what an ill report Folly has got, even among the most foolish), yet that I am that she, that only she, whose deity recreates both gods and men, even this is a sufficient argument, that I no sooner stepped up to speak to this full assembly than all your faces put on a kind of new and unwonted pleasantness.
full.author: Erasmus

What Folly does
The tone
rows: Introduces her family and companions and claims credit for youth, love, friendship and fun
Parades the foolish: hunters, gamblers, scholars, poets, philosophers, theologians, monks, rulers, popes
Says Christian faith itself looks like folly to the world, and that the greatest joy is a kind of holy madness
full.cap: The shape of the speech (our outline).

full.html: The middle part is the sharpest. Erasmus lets Folly mock scholars who argue over tiny questions, monks who care more for rules than for kindness, and church leaders who live like princes. He was a Catholic priest who wanted the church reformed from within, and these pages were read all over Europe.

full.text: In fine, I am so necessary to the making of all society and manner of life both delightful and lasting, that neither would the people long endure their governors, nor the servant his master, nor the master his footman, nor the scholar his tutor, nor one friend another, nor the wife her husband ... unless all of them had their interchangeable failings, one while flattering, other while prudently conniving, and generally sweetening one another with some small relish of folly.
full.author: Erasmus
full.note: Slightly shortened. "Conniving" here means kindly pretending not to notice.

full.html: Irony is the key to the book. The speaker is Folly, so we cannot simply believe her or simply dismiss her. Some of her praise is silly; some is a wise truth in a fool's costume. Readers have to decide, sentence by sentence, which is which.

In 1516 Erasmus published a printed edition of the Greek New Testament with a fresh Latin translation, a landmark of scholarship. A year later Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation. People said "Erasmus laid the egg that Luther hatched," because both criticized abuses in the church. But Erasmus stayed Catholic and disagreed with Luther in print, especially about free will. Many Protestants thought him too timid, and many Catholics thought him too critical, a position he accepted as the price of moderation.
Thinking satire means hatred. Erasmus teases the people he knew best: scholars like himself, churchmen like himself. Satire can come from love of what a thing ought to be.

deep.html: Folly belongs to a long line of wise fools: the jesters of royal courts, Shakespeare's Feste and Lear's Fool, and Cervantes's Sancho Panza, all later on this ladder. Behind them is St. Paul's line that God chose "the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1 Corinthians 1:27), which Folly quotes near the end.

items: Is a little foolishness necessary for friendship and family life? Where is the line between kindness and pretending?
Can you criticize an institution you love? What is the difference between reforming something and tearing it down?
Why might a writer let a fool say what he thinks, instead of saying it himself?

deep.html: Thomas More's Utopia (1516), written by Erasmus's friend, plays a similar game: a traveler describes a perfect island, and readers are left to decide how seriously to take it. Rabelais and Montaigne, next on this ladder, both read Erasmus closely.

questions: Folly says friends get along by overlooking each other's faults. Is that a good thing, or a kind of fib?
Which group that Folly teases would you most like to tease, and why?
How can you tell when someone is joking and when they mean it?
Erasmus stayed in his church while criticizing it. When is it better to stay and speak up, and when to leave?
Why do you think this little joke of a book became a best seller?
